excerpt: When someone other than your employer caused a work injury, you may have a claim beyond workers' compensation. How the two fit together.

faqs.question: What is a third-party claim for a work injury?
faqs.answer: It is a claim against a person or company other than your employer who caused your accident. It is separate from your workers' compensation claim, and you can pursue both at the same time.

faqs.question: Why can't I sue my employer directly?
faqs.answer: Workers' compensation is a no-fault system that pays medical expenses and replaces part of your wages without you having to prove your employer was negligent. The trade-off is that injured employees are usually barred from suing their employer.

faqs.question: What are common examples of third-party liability at work?
faqs.answer: Car accidents while driving a company vehicle or performing work tasks, injuries from defective tools or equipment, construction site accidents involving a general contractor, and injuries on someone else's property while making a work call.

faqs.question: Can I claim against a general contractor if I work for a subcontractor?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Construction sites bring together people from different companies, and the general contractor is typically responsible for safety on the jobsite, which can make them liable for an injury your own employer did not cause.

faqs.question: Do I lose my workers' compensation benefits if I bring a third-party claim?
faqs.answer: No. A third-party claim runs alongside your workers' compensation claim rather than replacing it. The two have different targets, different standards of proof, and different types of recoverable damages.
